[[File:Green Banks - Ewen-Purcell Horn Antenna info.jpg|right|thumb|upright=1.5|Plaque commemorating the discovery of 21-cm radiation from the Milky Way]]

'''Harold Irving "Doc" Ewen''' (March 5, 1922 – October 8, 2015) was an American physicist, radio astronomer, and business executive. He served in the [[United States Navy in World War II]] as a [[second lieutenant]]. As a graduate student under [[Edward M. Purcell]], he was the first to detect the galactic 21-cm [[hydrogen line]].

==Biography==
Ewen was born on March 5, 1922, in [[Chicopee, Massachusetts]],<ref name=Green_Bank/> son of S. Arthur Ewen and Ruth F. Fay. After an education at the Technical High School in [[Springfield, Massachusetts]],<ref name=Amherst_1951/> he matriculated at [[Amherst College]], studying undergraduate mathematics and astronomy,<ref name=Daniel/> and was awarded a B.A. in 1943.<ref name=Green_Bank/> With [[World War II]] underway, he joined the Navy.<ref name=Daniel/> Initially, he taught [[celestial navigation]] at Amherst as part of a pilot training program. Ewen received training in electronics and [[radar]] technology at [[Princeton University]] and [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]],<ref name=Bouton_Kellerman_2015/> then joined Navy airborne squadron 112, based in England, as a radar officer with the rank of [[Second Lieutenant]].<ref name=Stephan_1998/><ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/><ref name=Lang_2018/>

Following the war, Ewen began graduate studies at Harvard on the [[G.I. Bill]],<ref name=Lang_2018/> pursuing a degree in physics. He participated in the development of the 95-inch [[Harvard Cyclotron Laboratory|Harvard Cyclotron]].<ref name=Bouton_Kellerman_2015/> [[Edward Mills Purcell|Edward M. Purcell]] suggested that Ewen study prior work on the [[hyperfine]] line of [[neutral hydrogen]]. As a naval reserve officer, Ewen was able to obtain a translation of a 1945 paper by the Dutch astronomer [[Hendrik C. van de Hulst|H. C. van de Hulst]] on the subject. Van de Hulst expressed pessimism that such a signal would be detectable. Nonetheless, Ewen and Purcell agreed that his thesis topic should be to construct a [[microwave astronomy|microwave]] [[spectrometer]] to find a lower limit on the detectability of the 21-cm [[hydrogen line]].<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/>

With a $500 grant from the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences|AAA&S]], Ewen was able to purchase components to construct a pyramidal [[horn antenna]] and a 21-cm receiver. With the instrument assembled, a galactic 21-cm signal was successfully detected on March 25, 1951.<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/> This unexpected result was soon confirmed by Dutch and Australian astronomers.<ref name=Ewen_Purcell_1951/> Ewen was able to defend his thesis in May of that year, and he was awarded a Ph.D. from Harvard. He joined the [[Harvard Business School]] to pursue an [[Master of Business Administration|MBA]].<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/>

===Career===
In the fall of 1951, Ewen was called up to serve in the [[Korean War]].<ref name=Stephan_1998/> He remained for a month before negotiating his return to civilian life.<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/> He joined with [[Bart Bok]] as directors of the newly founded Harvard radio astronomy program during 1952–1958,<ref name=Brand_2002/> creating the nation's first Ph.D. program in this new field. During the 1950s, Ewen was involved in the planning for a national radio astronomy facility, and the site search for what would eventually become the [[Green Bank Telescope]] observatory.<ref name=Bouton_Kellerman_2015/>

Ewen joined with his friend Geoff Knight to launch the Ewen Knight Corporation in 1952, which was established to construct a hydrogen line receiver for Harvard at the [[George R. Agassiz Station|Agassiz Station]]. This company became a major supplier of equipment for radio observatories, including the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory|NRAO]].<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/> In 1956 he was married to Mary Ann Whitney;<ref name=Sullivan/> the couple would have seven children.<ref name=Daniel/> Ewen was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1957.<ref name=AAAS_1992/> He founded the Ewen Dae Corporation in 1958,<ref name=Green_Bank/> whose name was a play on [k]night and day and also became the initials of the couple's first child.<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/><ref name=Sullivan/>

Ewen devised a sextant-like radio direction finder that was used on submarines to find the position before firing missiles.<ref name=Kellerman_et_al_2020/> During 1989-1992 he was executive vice president at the [[Millitech Corporation]], becoming vice president for special projects, 1993–2000. At Millitech Corporation he was instrumental in winning and leading many significant programs.  These included several space programs, most notably [[Submillimeter Wave Astronomy Satellite]] (SWAS). SWAS was designed to study the chemical composition, energy balance and structure of [[Interstellar cloud|interstellar clouds]], both galactic and extragalactic, and investigate the processes of [[Nebular hypothesis|stellar and planetary formation]]. Ewen was also a pioneer in millimeter-wave passive imaging for multitude of applications, including weapon detection, defense and radioastronomy.{{cn|date=October 2025}} He served as president of E.K. Associates starting in 1992.<ref name=Bouton_Kellerman_2015/> In 2001, he became a research professor at the [[University of Massachusetts]]. Following his retirement, on November 12, 2002, Ewen gave the inaugural Gordon Lecture at the [[Arecibo Observatory]].<ref name=Brand_2002/> He was the technical operations director of Special Projects LLC in 2004.<ref name=Bouton_Kellerman_2015/>

In 1970, Ewen was given the [[IEEE Morris E. Leeds Award]] "for contributions to the design of sensitive radiometric systems, and for the codiscovery of the 21-cm spectral line of interstellar hydrogen".<ref name=Leeds_1970/> Ewen and Purcell were awarded the [[Beatrice M. Tinsley Prize]] in 1988 for the "first detection of 21-cm hyperfine transition radiation of neutral hydrogen".<ref name=Tinsley_1989/> The horn antenna used to detect the galaxy's 21-cm line from Harvard is now a [[historical marker]].<ref name=Marker/>
